# Style catalogue

<!-- generated by tools/build_data.py from synthesis/; edit the source, not this file -->

133 named visual styles, each placed on the same 15 trait axes. Plain words first, then the name designers use, then what stands out. This list is a map, not a fence: `references/style-lab.md` explains how to find a style from a person's words, mix two, change one trait, or explore new experimental ones with `engine.py style`. The first 28 are written up in depth, with real examples and code, in `references/styles.md`.

Columns: **Looks like** is the plain description; **Stands out** lists the traits that differ from a quiet neutral system; **Fits** is core-ui (product screens), marketing, or illustration-only.

## The 15 trait axes

Every style, named or new, is a choice on each axis. Bones (layout, density, type, scale, shape, theme) are what people read first, so experiments keep them typical; skin is where new looks spend their novelty. The plain words are what the engine says when it describes a style nobody has named yet.

- **surface** (skin; what a panel is made of): `solid` solid flat fills; `translucent` see-through frosted panels; `gradient` soft color blends; `metallic` metal and chrome; `glossy` shiny glossy surfaces; `luminous` surfaces that glow from inside
- **edge** (skin; how an edge is drawn (control edges always keep 3:1)): `none` no outlines; `hairline` thin hairline edges; `outline` clear outlines; `thick-outline` thick dark outlines; `beveled` raised beveled edges; `rough` rough hand-drawn edges
- **depth** (skin; how things lift off the page): `flat` no shadows; `ring` a faint outline and shadow; `tonal` lighter and darker layers; `soft-shadow` soft shadows that grow with height; `hard-offset` hard solid shadows like stickers; `extruded` shapes pushed out of the page; `inner` puffy shapes with inner shadows; `glass` frosted glass layers; `glow` a soft colored glow; `long-shadow` long flat shadows; `layered` stacked overlapping layers
- **shape** (bones; corners and shape language): `sharp` square corners; `subtle` slightly rounded corners; `rounded` rounded corners; `pill` pill-shaped controls; `blob` soft blobby shapes; `geometric` circles, squares and triangles; `irregular` wonky hand-made shapes; `pixel` blocky pixel shapes
- **color** (skin; how much color, and which kind): `monochrome` black, white and grays; `muted` quiet muted colors; `neutral-accent` grays with one accent; `tonal` shades of one color family; `vivid` bright bold colors; `neon` electric neon colors; `pastel` soft pastel colors; `earthy` earthy natural colors; `duotone` two strong colors; `spot-inks` two or three printing inks; `metallic` metal tones; `rainbow` many bright colors
- **contrast** (skin; how far apart lights and darks sit in the decoration; it never lowers text (4.5:1) or control (3:1) contrast): `low` gentle tones in the decoration; `normal` normal contrast; `high` stark high contrast
- **type** (bones; the letter style that carries the look (the font itself stays the person's choice)): `neo-grotesque` plain modern letters; `geometric` round geometric letters; `humanist` warm open letters; `serif` bookish serif letters; `slab` chunky slab letters; `rounded` soft rounded letters; `mono` code-style monospace letters; `pixel` pixel letters; `condensed` tall narrow letters; `display` characterful headline letters; `script` flowing script letters; `handwritten` handwritten letters; `blackletter` gothic blackletter
- **scale** (bones; the size jump between headlines and body text): `even` even, quiet type sizes; `moderate` a moderate size jump; `dramatic` huge headlines over small text
- **texture** (skin; a layer over flat color, kept off body text): `none` no texture; `grain` fine film grain; `halftone` comic dot shading; `scanlines` old-TV scanlines; `paper` paper fiber; `dither` dithered 1-bit dots; `pattern` repeating patterns; `glitch` glitchy broken pixels
- **imagery** (skin; what kind of pictures carry the look): `none` no pictures; `photo` photography; `illustration` drawn illustrations; `3d` 3D objects and scenes; `icon-led` icons instead of pictures; `type-only` type alone, no pictures
- **ornament** (skin; what decorates the page): `none` no decoration; `geometric-shapes` floating geometric shapes; `squiggles` squiggles and doodles; `stickers` sticker cut-outs; `ascii` text-made pictures; `ornamental` ornate decorative frames
- **layout** (bones; how the page is arranged): `grid` a tidy grid; `bento` boxes of different sizes; `editorial` a magazine layout; `asymmetric` an off-balance layout; `collage` a cut-and-paste collage; `full-bleed` edge-to-edge images; `layered` overlapping layers
- **density** (bones; how much fits on a screen; complexity costs first impressions most): `airy` lots of empty space; `balanced` a comfortable amount on screen; `dense` dense data screens
- **motion** (skin; the character of movement (reduced motion always gets a still version)): `still` almost no motion; `subtle` small quiet motion; `springy` springy motion; `bouncy` bouncy playful motion; `stepped` choppy frame-by-frame motion; `glitchy` glitchy jumps
- **theme** (bones; which theme is designed first; light and dark are always both built): `light-first` light screens first; `dark-first` dark screens first

Motion techniques are flags, not a look, because each carries its own accessibility rule: `parallax` layers moving at different speeds: a vestibular trigger, so reduced motion turns it off; `kinetic-type` moving type: reduced motion shows it still; `scroll-linked` motion tied to scrolling: reduced motion swaps it for a fade; `autoplay-loop` a loop that plays by itself: anything moving over 5 seconds needs pause (WCAG 2.2.2); `flashing` flashes: never more than three in any second (WCAG 2.3.1).
